_comment: Cosmic origin of each element, based on Jennifer A. Johnson's 'Origin of the Elements in the Solar System' (SDSS blog, 2017) and her 2020 review (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 378:20190301). Categories: big_bang, cosmic_rays, low_mass_stars, high_mass_stars (a.k.a. exploding massive stars / core-collapse SNe), white_dwarf_sn (Type Ia / exploding white dwarfs), neutron_star_merger (r-process), human_made. Elements with multiple sources list the dominant first; 'mix' captures all contributing processes for the overlay legend. Stories are short and student-facing, not academic.

H.story: Almost all hydrogen formed in the first three minutes after the Big Bang. The hydrogen in the water you drink — and in every cell of your body — is essentially that old.

He.story: Most helium is primordial, formed in the first minutes after the Big Bang. Stars produce more by fusing hydrogen, but the Big Bang did most of the work.

Li.story: A trace of lithium formed in the Big Bang, some is made when cosmic rays smash heavier nuclei, but most of the lithium around today was made in dying low-mass stars.

Be.story: Beryllium is made almost entirely by cosmic-ray fission — high-energy particles slamming into bigger nuclei and chipping them apart in interstellar space.

B.story: Like beryllium, boron is mostly the wreckage of cosmic rays breaking up heavier atoms in space. Stars actually destroy boron more than they make it.

C.story: Carbon is forged in red-giant stars by the triple-alpha process — three helium nuclei fusing into one carbon. Every carbon atom in your body was made inside a star that died before the Sun was born.

N.story: Nitrogen is made mostly in dying low-mass stars through the CNO cycle. The nitrogen in your DNA started its life in a star.

O.story: Oxygen is forged in the cores of massive stars and scattered when they explode as supernovae. The oxygen you're breathing right now came from stellar explosions long before Earth existed.

F.story: Fluorine is rare and its origin is debated, but most comes from massive stars and from a special neutrino-driven process during supernova explosions.

Ne.story: Neon is produced in the carbon-burning layers of massive stars and released when those stars explode as supernovae.

Na.story: Sodium is made primarily in massive stars during carbon burning and dispersed by supernovae. The sodium in your blood came from exploded stars.

Mg.story: Magnesium is forged in massive stars and scattered in supernovae. The magnesium at the heart of every chlorophyll molecule was once inside a star.

Al.story: Aluminum is produced in the neon- and carbon-burning shells of massive stars and ejected by core-collapse supernovae.

Si.story: Silicon is one of the main products of massive-star fusion and also comes from exploding white dwarfs. The silicon in every grain of sand was made in dying stars.

P.story: Phosphorus is produced in massive stars during oxygen and neon burning. Every phosphorus atom in your DNA backbone was made in a stellar explosion.

S.story: Sulfur is forged in the silicon-burning stages of massive stars and in white-dwarf supernovae.

Cl.story: Chlorine is produced mostly by massive stars and dispersed in their supernova explosions. The salt on your food contains atoms once at the heart of a dying star.

Ar.story: Argon comes mainly from oxygen burning in massive stars, with some contribution from exploding white dwarfs.

K.story: Potassium is mostly made in massive stars. The potassium pumping through every nerve in your body started in a supernova.

Ca.story: Calcium is forged during silicon burning in massive stars and in exploding white dwarfs. The calcium in your bones and teeth was made in stellar explosions.

Sc.story: Scandium is a rare element made mostly in massive stars during their late burning stages.

Ti.story: Titanium is produced largely by exploding white dwarfs (Type Ia supernovae) and partly by massive stars.

V.story: Vanadium comes mostly from white-dwarf supernovae, with a contribution from massive-star explosions.

Cr.story: Chromium is produced mostly by exploding white dwarfs. The chromium that makes stainless steel rust-resistant has explosive origins.

Mn.story: Manganese is made primarily in white-dwarf supernovae — the runaway thermonuclear explosions of dead stars.

Fe.story: Most iron in the universe is forged in exploding white dwarfs. The iron in your blood that carries oxygen was made in stellar explosions billions of years ago.

Co.story: Cobalt is produced in massive-star supernovae and white-dwarf explosions. It's named after a German word for goblin — miners blamed it for spoiling their silver ore.

Ni.story: Nickel, like iron, is made primarily in white-dwarf supernovae. Most of it is born as radioactive Ni-56 that decays into iron.

Cu.story: Copper is made in massive stars and partly in dying low-mass stars. The copper in every wire and circuit was forged in stars.

Zn.story: Zinc is produced mostly in massive-star supernovae, with some contribution from low-mass stars.

Ga.story: Gallium is made mostly in dying low-mass stars through slow neutron capture (the s-process).

Ge.story: Germanium is forged primarily by neutron capture in dying low-mass stars.

As.story: Arsenic comes from a mix of massive-star and low-mass-star nucleosynthesis. Its toxicity to life made it infamous long before chemists understood why.

Se.story: Selenium is produced by neutron capture in both massive and low-mass dying stars.

Br.story: Bromine is made mostly through rapid neutron capture in massive-star supernovae.

Kr.story: Krypton is split between the slow neutron-capture process in low-mass stars and the rapid process in supernovae.

Rb.story: Rubidium is produced mostly by slow neutron capture in dying low-mass stars.

Sr.story: Strontium is made dominantly in dying low-mass stars. It's what makes red fireworks red.

Y.story: Yttrium is produced largely by the slow neutron-capture process in dying low-mass stars.

Zr.story: Zirconium is forged mostly in dying low-mass stars through neutron capture.

Nb.story: Niobium is made mostly in dying low-mass stars by the slow neutron-capture process.

Mo.story: Molybdenum is built up by neutron capture in dying low-mass stars, with additional contributions from supernovae and neutron-star mergers.

Tc.story: Technetium has no stable isotopes — every atom decays. Detection of technetium in red-giant stars in 1952 was direct proof that stars make heavy elements. On Earth, essentially all of it is synthetic, produced in reactors and used in medical imaging.

Ru.story: Ruthenium is produced by neutron capture in dying low-mass stars and in neutron-star mergers.

Rh.story: Rhodium is forged largely in the violent merger of two neutron stars — one of the rarest events in the universe.

Pd.story: Palladium is produced by neutron capture in dying low-mass stars and in neutron-star mergers.

Ag.story: Most silver was forged when two neutron stars collided. Your jewelry contains atoms made in cosmic cataclysms older than the Sun.

Cd.story: Cadmium is made primarily by slow neutron capture in dying low-mass stars.

In.story: Indium is produced mostly in neutron-star mergers. The indium-tin oxide on every touchscreen has cataclysmic origins.

Sn.story: Tin is built up mostly by slow neutron capture in dying low-mass stars.

Sb.story: Antimony is produced largely by rapid neutron capture in neutron-star mergers.

Te.story: Most tellurium was made in neutron-star mergers — the violent collision of two collapsed stellar cores.

I.story: Iodine is forged mostly in neutron-star mergers. The iodine your thyroid needs was made in cosmic collisions.

Xe.story: Xenon has roughly equal contributions from slow neutron capture in low-mass stars and rapid capture in neutron-star mergers.

Cs.story: Cesium is made primarily by slow neutron capture in dying low-mass stars.

Ba.story: Barium is produced mostly in dying low-mass stars and is a key diagnostic element for stellar nucleosynthesis.

La.story: Lanthanum is made largely by the slow neutron-capture process in dying low-mass stars.

Ce.story: Cerium is the most abundant rare-earth element on Earth, mostly produced in dying low-mass stars.

Pr.story: Praseodymium is built up mostly through slow neutron capture in dying low-mass stars.

Nd.story: Neodymium is forged mostly in dying low-mass stars. The neodymium magnets in your headphones have stellar origins.

Pm.story: Promethium has no stable isotopes — all decay quickly. Like technetium, every atom of it on Earth was made by humans, mostly in nuclear reactors as a fission product.

Sm.story: Samarium is produced by neutron capture in dying low-mass stars and in neutron-star mergers.

Eu.story: Most europium was forged in neutron-star mergers — it's one of the cleanest tracers of the rapid neutron-capture process in the universe.

Gd.story: Gadolinium is produced largely in neutron-star mergers by rapid neutron capture.

Tb.story: Terbium comes mostly from neutron-star mergers — the cosmos's heaviest-element foundries.

Dy.story: Dysprosium is forged predominantly in neutron-star mergers.

Ho.story: Holmium is produced mostly by rapid neutron capture during the collision of two neutron stars.

Er.story: Erbium is built up primarily in neutron-star mergers.

Tm.story: Thulium, the rarest of the stable rare-earth elements, is made mostly in neutron-star mergers.

Yb.story: Ytterbium has roughly equal contributions from dying low-mass stars and neutron-star mergers.

Lu.story: Lutetium is produced mostly in neutron-star mergers.

Hf.story: Hafnium is made largely by slow neutron capture in dying low-mass stars.

Ta.story: Tantalum is forged primarily in dying low-mass stars by neutron capture.

W.story: Tungsten is built up mostly in dying low-mass stars. With the highest melting point of any metal, it makes light-bulb filaments and drill bits.

Re.story: Rhenium is one of the rarest stable elements, made mostly in neutron-star mergers.

Os.story: Osmium, the densest natural element, is forged mostly in the collision of neutron stars.

Ir.story: Iridium is produced mostly in neutron-star mergers. A worldwide iridium layer in Earth's rocks is the smoking gun for the asteroid impact that killed the dinosaurs.

Pt.story: Platinum was largely made when two neutron stars collided. Every platinum atom in a catalytic converter has cataclysmic origins.

Au.story: Most gold in the universe was forged in the collision of two neutron stars. The gold in any wedding ring you own is older than the Sun itself.

Hg.story: Mercury is produced mostly by slow neutron capture in dying low-mass stars.

Tl.story: Thallium is made largely in dying low-mass stars through neutron capture.

Pb.story: Most lead in the universe was forged in dying low-mass stars, the terminus of the slow neutron-capture process. The rest comes from radioactive decay of uranium and thorium.

Bi.story: Bismuth is the heaviest element produced by slow neutron capture in dying low-mass stars.

Po.story: Polonium exists today as a radioactive intermediate in the decay chains of heavier elements like uranium. Those parent elements came from neutron-star mergers.

At.story: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth — at any moment, less than a teaspoon's worth exists in the entire crust, all from decay of heavier nuclei made in neutron-star mergers.

Rn.story: Radon is a decay product of uranium and thorium. It seeps from soil and is the leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers. Its parents were forged in neutron-star mergers.

Fr.story: Francium has the second-shortest half-life of any naturally occurring element. The atoms that exist now are decay products of actinium, ultimately from neutron-star mergers.

Ra.story: Radium is a decay product of uranium. Marie Curie isolated it in 1898 by working through tons of pitchblende — and paid for the discovery with her life.

Ac.story: Actinium is a decay product of uranium, ultimately from r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron-star mergers.

Th.story: Thorium is forged in neutron-star mergers. With a half-life of 14 billion years, the thorium in Earth's crust is original — it predates the Solar System.

Pa.story: Protactinium exists only as a decay intermediate of uranium and thorium, themselves from neutron-star mergers.

U.story: Uranium was forged in neutron-star mergers. The uranium powering nuclear reactors today is original cosmic material — it was here when Earth formed 4.5 billion years ago.

Np.story: Neptunium occurs in only trace amounts in nature. Essentially all of it is synthetic, produced as a by-product in nuclear reactors. It was the first transuranium element discovered, in 1940.

Pu.story: Plutonium is overwhelmingly man-made. Trace natural plutonium exists, but every gram in reactors and weapons was bred in nuclear reactors from uranium.

Am.story: Americium is entirely synthetic, made in nuclear reactors. A microgram of it sits inside most household smoke detectors.

Cm.story: Curium is named after Marie and Pierre Curie. Like all transuranium elements past plutonium, it exists only because humans made it in reactors and accelerators.

Bk.story: Berkelium, named for Berkeley, California, is produced only in tiny quantities in high-flux nuclear reactors.

Cf.story: Californium is one of the heaviest elements made in usable quantities — and one of the most expensive substances on Earth, at tens of millions of dollars per gram.

Es.story: Einsteinium was first discovered in the fallout of the first hydrogen-bomb test in 1952. Today it's made in microgram quantities in research reactors.

Fm.story: Fermium, like einsteinium, was first found in thermonuclear test debris. It can only be made in nuclear reactors and accelerators.

Md.story: Mendelevium, named for Dmitri Mendeleev, is made one atom at a time in particle accelerators by bombarding einsteinium with alpha particles.

No.story: Nobelium is produced atom-by-atom in heavy-ion accelerators. No macroscopic sample has ever existed.

Lr.story: Lawrencium is named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron. It's made one atom at a time in accelerators and decays within minutes.

Rf.story: Rutherfordium is a synthetic superheavy element. Atoms are produced in particle accelerators and decay in seconds.

Db.story: Dubnium is named for Dubna, Russia, one of the labs that races to create superheavy elements. Only handfuls of atoms have ever been made.

Sg.story: Seaborgium is named after Glenn Seaborg, who discovered ten transuranium elements. It exists only as a few atoms made in accelerators.

Bh.story: Bohrium, named after Niels Bohr, is a synthetic element produced one atom at a time in heavy-ion collisions.

Hs.story: Hassium is named for the German state of Hesse. Atoms of it exist for only seconds before decaying.

Mt.story: Meitnerium honors Lise Meitner, who co-discovered nuclear fission. It's been made only as a handful of fleeting atoms.

Ds.story: Darmstadtium is named for Darmstadt, Germany, where it was first made. It's purely synthetic and extremely short-lived.

Rg.story: Roentgenium honors Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays. It's made one atom at a time in particle accelerators.

Cn.story: Copernicium is named after Nicolaus Copernicus. Like all superheavy elements, it's synthetic and exists for only fractions of a second.

Nh.story: Nihonium was created in Japan in 2004 — the first element discovered in East Asia. Its name comes from 'Nihon', meaning Japan.

Fl.story: Flerovium is named for Russian physicist Georgy Flyorov. Atoms of it exist for less than a second before decaying.

Mc.story: Moscovium was created at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research near Moscow. It's purely synthetic and extraordinarily short-lived.

Lv.story: Livermorium is named after Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California. It's produced only as a few atoms in accelerator experiments.

Ts.story: Tennessine is named for Tennessee, home to Oak Ridge National Laboratory. It was first synthesized in 2010 and only a handful of atoms have ever existed.

Og.story: Oganesson, the heaviest known element, is named for physicist Yuri Oganessian. Fewer than ten atoms of it have ever been detected, each existing for less than a millisecond.
